cards.headline: Three financial statements reveal a company's health
cards.one_thing: Each financial statement shows a distinct aspect: position, performance, and cash movement
cards.narration: This is the first session of the week. Today introduces three core financial statements: balance sheet (position), income statement (performance), and cash flow statement (cash movement). Using Financial Intelligence for Entrepreneurs (pages 1-20), Mash Direct Ltd's FY2025 accounts will illustrate how these statements interrelate. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities, and equity; the income statement lists revenues and expenses; the cash flow statement tracks operating, investing, and financing activities.

ideas.label: Structure

ideas.label: Link

cards.headline: Mash Direct Ltd's P&L Mechanics: Revenue, Expenses, Profit
cards.one_thing: Revenue recognition, expense categorisation, and net profit calculation form the core of the income statement.
cards.narration: Yesterday established the three financial statements' roles. Today, using Mash Direct Ltd's FY2025 data, we focus on the income statement. Revenue is recognised when earned, not received. Expenses are split into operating (e.g., salaries) and non-operating (e.g., interest). Net profit is total revenue minus all expenses. This builds on yesterday's understanding of how statements interrelate.

ideas.label: Revenue Recognition
ideas.text: Recognise revenue when earned, not received.

ideas.label: Expense Categorisation
ideas.text: Classify expenses as operating (e.g., salaries) or non-operating (e.g., interest).

ideas.label: Net Profit Calculation
ideas.text: Subtract total expenses from total revenue to determine net profit.

example.takeaway: Net profit (£60,000) reflects all expenses, showing true profitability.

flow.note: Use FY2025 data from Mash Direct Ltd.

cards.headline: Income Statement Drives Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Changes
cards.one_thing: Net income increases retained earnings (balance sheet) and operating cash flow (cash flow statement).
cards.narration: Yesterday covered P&L basics. Today, focus on how income statement items directly impact balance sheet equity and cash flow. Using Around Noon Ltd's FY2024 data from pages 41-60 of *Financial Intelligence for Entrepreneurs*, examine how revenues, expenses, and depreciation flow between statements. For example, net income reduces cash flow but increases retained earnings, while depreciation lowers cash flow without affecting profit.

ideas.label: Retained Earnings
ideas.text: Net income increases retained earnings on the balance sheet.

ideas.label: Depreciation
ideas.text: Depreciation reduces cash flow but not net income.

ideas.label: Operating Expenses
ideas.text: Higher operating expenses lower both net income and cash flow.

example.title: Around Noon Ltd FY2024 Illustration
example.takeaway: Net income flows to retained earnings and operating cash flow, while depreciation and expenses reduce cash flow.

flow.note: Add net income to retained earnings.
